y0: Those Who Speak but Do Not Act
y1: Jesus says that the teachers of the law and the Pharisees “sit on Moses' seat”, so obey their teaching, but do not follow their example. “For they say, and don't do.”
y2: They make their phylacteries broad, lengthen the fringes of their garments, and love the place of honor at feasts and the title “Rabbi”. Jesus says, “You have one Teacher, and you are all brothers,” reiterating that the greatest is the one who serves (20:26).
y3: In 23:13–36, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!” is repeated seven times. This structure contrasts with the Beatitudes in chapter 5. There are strong metaphors like straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel, a cup clean on the outside but dirty inside, and whitewashed tombs.
y4: The Wings of a Mother Hen
y5: At the end of the seven warnings, Jesus' tone changes. “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets, and stones those who are sent to her!” Behind the anger were tears.
y6: “How often I would have gathered your children together, even as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!” God does not embrace by force. He respects even the freedom to reject the invitation.
y7: The Bible also depicts God as an eagle (Deut. 32:11) and a mother (Isa. 66:13). The image of taking refuge under wings frequently appears in the Psalms (91:4). Jesus applies this embrace of God to Himself.
y9: Some of the stones of Herod's temple were over 12 meters long. When the disciples marveled, Jesus says: “There will not be left here one stone on another, that will not be thrown down.” This prophecy was fulfilled exactly as spoken by the Roman army in AD 70.
y10: On the Mount of Olives, Jesus speaks of false christs, wars, famines, earthquakes, and persecutions, saying: “These things must happen, but the end is not yet,” and “these are the beginning of birth pains.” And: “This Good News of the Kingdom will be preached in the whole world for a testimony to all the nations, and then the end will come.”
y11: In chapter 24, the near future (the destruction of the temple in AD 70) and the distant future (Jesus' second coming) overlap. The purpose is not to calculate dates, but to not be deceived, not fear, endure to the end, and spread the Gospel.
y13: “But no one knows of that day and hour, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father alone.” Just as in the days of Noah, people will be eating and drinking when it suddenly comes upon them. Therefore, “keep watch.”
y14: Keeping watch is not staring at the sky all night. The servant who gives the household “their food in due season” as entrusted by the master is the watchful servant. He is contrasted with the servant who beats his fellow servants and drinks with drunkards because the master is delayed.
y15: Unlike the cursed tree in chapter 21, the fig tree in 24:32 is a sign of hope. Just as summer is near when its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, the completion of the kingdom of heaven will surely come.
verse: “Watch therefore, for you don't know in what hour your Lord comes. … Therefore also be ready, for in an hour that you don't expect, the Son of Man will come.”
prayer: Jesus, thank You for Your heart that wept for Jerusalem even as You rebuked hypocrisy. Let me live with a serving faith, not one for show. Let me return under the wings of the hen, wait for Your coming with hope instead of fear, and be faithful in the work You have entrusted to me. I pray in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.
d0: phylactery. They were small leather boxes containing Bible verses, tied to the forehead and arm (Deut. 6:8). They made them large to show off their piety. Even today, orthodox Jews wear phylacteries when they pray.
d1: want. Jesus says, “I would have... and you would not.” God's love does not force. The same verb is in 8:3, “I want to. Be made clean.”
d2: keep watch. To wait without falling asleep. In Gethsemane, Jesus told His disciples to “keep watch”, but they fell asleep (26:38–41). The name Gregory comes from this word.
